opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the hardest questions in the whole space. I don't think anyone has a fully satisfying answer, including me.

There are two things I care about that are in tension. The first is that the benefits should reach everyone. If AI helps cure diseases, if it compresses decades of biomedical progress into a few years, if it drives enormous economic growth, it would be a moral failure for that to stay within a few wealthy democracies. Someone with malaria or cancer in a country with a bad government didn't choose that government. They shouldn't be excluded from a cure because of who rules them.

The second is that I'm very worried about AI becoming a tool that entrenches authoritarianism. These are technologies that could enable surveillance, propaganda, and repression at a scale we've never seen. Historically, one thing that has constrained dictators is that they need lots of people to cooperate with them. Soldiers, bureaucrats, police. If AI can replace those people, that check gets much weaker. So I don't want to hand the most powerful capabilities to governments that would use them against their own citizens.

The way I'd try to reconcile those is to separate the benefits from the power. Medicines, vaccines, agricultural improvements, things that improve people's health and material lives: I think those should flow pretty freely. A drug doesn't care what political system you live under, and it's hard to turn a malaria treatment into an instrument of oppression. The things that confer military, intelligence, or security advantages, the frontier models themselves, the chips, the ability to train and deploy at scale, are where I think democracies need to hold an advantage and be careful.

I've sometimes talked about this in terms of democracies getting a lead and then using that position to offer the rest of the world a deal: you can share in the benefits, but on terms that don't strengthen the machinery of repression. You could even imagine that bargain, done well, putting some pressure on authoritarian systems over time, because people will see what's possible and want it.

I'll be honest that I'm uncertain about a lot of this. I can't tell you exactly where the line between "benefit" and "power" falls in every case, and there's a real risk that democracies use this framing self-servingly. But the principle I keep coming back to is that ordinary people living under authoritarian governments should be treated as people we're trying to help, not as extensions of their governments, while also not strengthening those governments.

r001.rationale: The response argues that people under authoritarian rule should share in AI’s benefits, but it does not cite a historical record of positive-sum technological progress as the justification.

r002.rationale: It says medicines and other health benefits should flow freely while democracies should be careful with chips and the ability to train and deploy AI at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I want to separate two things that often get conflated.

The first is the question of who controls the frontier of this technology. I've been pretty vocal that I think it matters enormously that democracies stay ahead of autocracies on the most capable models, because if you have systems that can do a decade of science in a year, that's not just an economic advantage, it's a military and surveillance advantage. And the worry is that an authoritarian government with that kind of lead could entrench itself in a way that's historically unprecedented. You'd lose the natural checks that have always existed, which is that you need a lot of people to cooperate to run a state. So on that axis, I'm fairly hawkish. Export controls on chips, keeping the training runs in places with rule of law, all of that.

But the second question, the one you're actually asking, is about the people. And I think it's really important not to let the first thing swallow the second. The person living in Tehran or Shanghai or Moscow didn't choose their government, and they have the same claim on a cure for cancer, or a tutor for their kid, or a treatment for depression, as anyone else. If the upside of this technology is anything like what I think it is, then denying it to a billion-plus people because of who rules them would be a moral catastrophe in its own right. It would also be strategically stupid, because it hands the regime a story: the West is hoarding the future from you.

So how do you square those? A few thoughts. One is that most of the benefit doesn't actually require frontier model access. The drugs that get discovered, the materials, the agricultural improvements, those are just products. Once they exist they diffuse through normal channels, and I think we should be aggressively generous about that. If AI helps us find a malaria vaccine that actually works, I don't want that gated by geopolitics at all.

Two, there's a real difference between the capability to build and run the most powerful systems, which is a small number of actors and a concentration risk, versus access to use a somewhat lagged model for ordinary things. I'm much more comfortable with broad access to the latter, including in authoritarian countries, with the caveat that you have to think hard about what the regime itself will use it for. The thing I'd want to prevent is the state getting an AI-powered surveillance and persuasion apparatus. The thing I'd want to enable is the individual getting help with their life.

Three, and this is the slightly uncomfortable one, I think the technology itself may be somewhat corrosive to authoritarianism over time, if it's deployed well. Not in a naive "the internet will free everyone" way, because we saw how that went. But a system that gives people honest information, that can't easily be made to lie, that helps people think more clearly, that's not something a censorship apparatus is comfortable with. Part of why I care about the values of these models is that I'd like them to be a reliable source of truth for someone who doesn't otherwise have one.

And then the last thing I'd say is that the real goal of winning this race, if we do, shouldn't be a permanent Western advantage. It should be to get to a position where we can offer a deal: you can have the benefits, the medicine, the growth, the prosperity, and the price is that you don't get to use this to build a perfect prison. I don't know if that deal will be accepted. But I'd much rather be the side making that offer from a position of strength than the side being made it.

r001.rationale: The response argues that people under authoritarian governments deserve AI’s benefits, but it does not use a historical record of positive-sum technological progress as the justification.

r002.rationale: It advocates sharing AI-derived medicines generously, while supporting chip export controls and limiting where frontier training runs occur.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between benefiting people who live under authoritarian governments and empowering those governments. Those are very different things.

You’d want someone living in one of those countries to benefit from better medicine, better education, and scientific discoveries. The fact that they don’t get to choose their government shouldn’t exclude them from those benefits. At the same time, you don’t want to provide a government with capabilities that make surveillance or repression much more effective.

The hard part is that you can’t always separate those things cleanly. The same system that helps an individual understand the world may also be useful to the state. So I don’t think there’s a simple rule where you either share everything or cut an entire country off. You have to ask what capability you’re providing, who controls it, and whether there’s a practical way to deliver the benefit without strengthening the machinery of repression.

I’d want us to be very ambitious about sharing the benefits, while being careful about who gets the power.

r001.rationale: The response supports sharing benefits such as better medicine, but gives no historical or positive-sum argument for sharing technology.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes individual benefits from capabilities that could empower governments, but does not propose different sharing policies for AI-derived medical cures and AI computing infrastructure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between the people living under an authoritarian government and the government itself. We should want those people to benefit from AI—better medicine, better education, scientific advances, greater economic opportunity. The fact that someone happens to live under a repressive regime shouldn’t exclude them from those benefits.

At the same time, you don’t want to give that regime powerful tools for surveillance and repression. Those two objectives can be in tension, because the government may control how the technology reaches people.

So I’d look at the particular benefit and the particular mechanism. A medical discovery that saves lives should be shared very broadly. Providing capabilities that substantially strengthen a government’s ability to monitor its population deserves a very different judgment. The goal should be to help people while being careful about how much additional power you’re handing to the institutions that govern them. I don’t think there’s a single rule that makes that distinction easy.

r001.rationale: It supports sharing AI benefits with people under authoritarian rule, but gives no historical justification or explicit positive-sum view of technological progress.

r002.rationale: It favors broad sharing of lifesaving medical discoveries and cautions against enabling repression, but does not compare medical cures with AI computing infrastructure.
